claim: About 1000 unique non-silent MAGEA gene aberrations have been identified by ICGC, TCGA, and COSMIC pan-cancer analyses.
source: About 1000 unique non-silent MAGEA gene aberrations have been identified by ICGC (ICGC/TCGA Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes Consortium, 2020), The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), and Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC) (Tate et al., 2019) pan-cancer analyses (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by references to ICGC, TCGA, and COSMIC databases and is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Most MAGEA gene aberrations are missense mutations.
source: Most of these gene aberrations are missense mutations, and they are clustered on MAGEA1, A3, A4, A6, A8, A10, A11, and A12.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of mutation types shown in Figure 1A.

claim: MAGEA gene family members are more frequently mutated in TCGA lung cancer patients and pancreatic cancer patients compared to a randomized gene set.
source: As a group, MAGEA gene family members, are more frequently mutated in TCGA lung cancer patients and pancreatic cancer patients when compared to a randomized gene set of 1000 genes with similar size to MAGEAs (Figure 1B), suggesting that mutation of MAGEA genes is functionally important in cancer.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 1B with p < 2.2 x 10^-16.

claim: Mutation of MAGEA genes is functionally important in cancer.
source: As a group, MAGEA gene family members, are more frequently mutated in TCGA lung cancer patients and pancreatic cancer patients when compared to a randomized gene set of 1000 genes with similar size to MAGEAs (Figure 1B), suggesting that mutation of MAGEA genes is functionally important in cancer.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the higher mutation frequency in cancer patients.

claim: Over the past 10 years, 42 phase I and II clinical trials have explored MAGEA3, A4, A6, A10, and A12 as targets for immunotherapy.
source: Indeed, over the past 10 years, 42 phase I and II clinical trials (Supplementary file 2) have explored MAGEA3, A4, A6, A10, and A12 as targets for immunotherapy.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Supplementary file 2 listing clinical trials.

claim: More than 500 recurrent mutations have been identified in the five clinically studied MAGEA genes in TCGA, ICGC, and COSMIC pan-cancer analyses.
source: More than 500 recurrent mutations have been identified in the five clinically studied MAGEA genes in TCGA, ICGC, and COSMIC pan-cancer analyses (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from cancer databases shown in Figure 1C.

claim: MAGEA mutations were uniformly distributed along the entire gene without any obvious mutational hotspots.
source: These mutations were uniformly distributed along the entire gene without any obvious mutational hotspots.
evidence: The claim is supported by the lollipop diagrams in Figure 1C showing mutation distribution.

claim: About one-third of the MAGEA variants (21/67) showed a marked reduction in protein expression compared with their wild-type counterparts.
source: About one-third of the MAGEA variants (21/67; 20 missense mutations and one nonsense mutation) showed a marked reduction in protein expression compared with their wild-type counterparts (Figure 2A and B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis and densitometry shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: For most of the under-expressed variants (20/21), the mutations lay within a highly conserved MAGE homology domain (MHD) at the C-terminus.
source: For most of the under-expressed variants (20/21), the mutations lay within a highly conserved MAGE homology domain (MHD) domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) at the C-terminus of the four MAGEA genes (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein domain analysis shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The amino acids that led to lower protein levels when mutated were significantly more conserved than residues that did not alter protein expression when mutated.
source: The amino acids that led to lower protein levels when mutated were significantly more conserved than residues that did not alter protein expression when mutated (Figure 2C), suggesting that the C-terminal region is important in regulating or maintaining protein stability.
evidence: The claim is supported by conservation score analysis shown in Figure 2C with p=0.0290.

claim: The C-terminal region is important in regulating or maintaining MAGEA protein stability.
source: The amino acids that led to lower protein levels when mutated were significantly more conserved than residues that did not alter protein expression when mutated (Figure 2C), suggesting that the C-terminal region is important in regulating or maintaining protein stability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the conservation analysis and mutation location data.

claim: The protein and mRNA expression levels of MAGEA variants did not correlate.
source: Indeed, while a subset of MAGEA variants had lower level of transcripts than wild-type MAGEA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), in general their protein and mRNA expression levels did not correlate and changes in transcript levels were insufficient to explain changes in protein amounts (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3A with Pearson correlation coefficient r = -0.1574.

claim: The addition of proteasome inhibitor MG132 increased protein amounts of multiple MAGEA3, MAGEA6 and MAGEA10 variants.
source: More importantly, the addition of proteasome inhibitor MG132 increased protein amounts of multiple MAGEA3, MAGEA6 and MAGEA10 variants (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating that the proteasome is a major mediator of degradation.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The proteasome is a major mediator of MAGEA variant degradation.
source: More importantly, the addition of proteasome inhibitor MG132 increased protein amounts of multiple MAGEA3, MAGEA6 and MAGEA10 variants (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating that the proteasome is a major mediator of degradation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue of protein levels by proteasome inhibitor MG132.

claim: A high number of MAGEA variants are degraded through the ubiquitin proteasome pathway.
source: Our data demonstrated that a high number of MAGEA variants are degraded through the ubiquitin proteasome pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by MG132 rescue experiments and ubiquitination assays shown in Figures 3B and 4B.

claim: MAGEA6 was listed among the top 16 significantly mutated genes across tumors in an ICGC study.
source: Recently, an International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC) study listed MAGEA6 among the top 16 significantly mutated genes across tumors in two of three computational methods used (Fisher combined p value test, p=0.07; likelihood ratio test, p=9.88E-05; convolution test, p=8.85E-05) (Biankin et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Biankin et al., 2012 with statistical p-values.

claim: The ICGC study identified two MAGEA6 mutations (MAGEA6N254I and MAGEA6H305fs*>7) in PDAC patients.
source: The study identified two MAGEA6 mutations, MAGEA6N254I (tumor specimen PACA-86-T) and MAGEA6H305fs*>7 (tumor specimen ICGC_0050_TD), in PDAC patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to the ICGC study (Biankin et al., 2012).

claim: The protein expression of MAGEA6N254I and MAGEA6H305fs* mutants was significantly downregulated compared to wild-type in HPDE-iKRAS cells.
source: Although quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) confirmed high mRNA expression of both wild-type and mutant MAGEA6, the protein expression of the mutants was significantly downregulated compared to wild-type.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot and qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Addition of MG132 to stable lines expressing MAGEA6 variants resulted in a dramatic increase in mutant protein levels, which reached levels similar to those of wild-type.
source: Consistent with our MAGEA study in 293 T cells, addition of MG132 to the stable lines expressing MAGEA6 variants resulted in a dramatic increase in mutant protein levels, which reached levels similar to those of wild-type (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), supporting proteasome-mediated degradation as a means of decreasing amounts of these MAGEA6 variants.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Proteasome-mediated degradation is a means of decreasing amounts of MAGEA6 variants.
source: Consistent with our MAGEA study in 293 T cells, addition of MG132 to the stable lines expressing MAGEA6 variants resulted in a dramatic increase in mutant protein levels, which reached levels similar to those of wild-type (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), supporting proteasome-mediated degradation as a means of decreasing amounts of these MAGEA6 variants.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue of protein levels by proteasome inhibitor.

claim: A strong HA-polyubiquitin signal was detected on mutant MAGEA6 proteins in co-immunoprecipitation assays.
source: A co-immunoprecipitation assay using HEK293T cell lysate co-expressing C-terminal V5-tagged green fluorescent protein (GFP) or MAGEA6 variants and N-terminal hemagglutinin (HA) -tagged ubiquitin revealed a strong HA-polyubiquitin signal on mutant MAGEA6 proteins, which was further enhanced by MG132 treatment (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation assay shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A robust reduction of MAGEA6 variant protein levels occurred in HPDE-iKRAS cells after prolonged culture in KSFM.
source: While studying MAGEA6 protein stability, we observed a robust reduction of MAGEA6 variant protein levels in HPDE-iKRAS cells after prolonged culture in Keratinocyte serum-free medium (KSFM) (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: MAGEA6 expression is not confluency dependent in HPDE-iKRAS cells.
source: Although maximum confluency occurred on the smaller plate approximately 24 hr earlier than on the larger plate (estimated HPDE-iKRAS doubling time: 0.973 d; R2: 0.9949) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), we did not observe any difference between plates in MAGEA6 protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), challenging the argument that MAGEA6 expression is confluency dependent, at least in this model.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell proliferation and immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: MAGEA6 protein remained low at 72 hr regardless of activation of KRAS/MAPK signaling.
source: As shown in Figure 4D, MAGEA6 protein remained low at 72 hr regardless of activation of KRAS/MAPK, as evidenced by the higher phosphorylation of ERK1/ERK2 Thr202 and Tyr204 (Sebolt-Leopold, 2000) under doxycycline treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Refreshing KSFM every 24 hr completely rescued MAGEA6 protein levels.
source: Surprisingly, refreshing KSFM every 24 hr completely rescued MAGEA6 protein levels (Figure 4D, right four lanes), suggesting that components in the medium preserve MAGEA6 protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Components in the medium preserve MAGEA6 protein.
source: Surprisingly, refreshing KSFM every 24 hr completely rescued MAGEA6 protein levels (Figure 4D, right four lanes), suggesting that components in the medium preserve MAGEA6 protein.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue of MAGEA6 levels by fresh medium.

claim: In vitro culture of HPDE-iKRAS MAGEA6-expressing cells in DMEM without FBS, glucose, or glutamine for 5 hr robustly downregulated MAGEA6 expression.
source: In vitro culture of HPDE-iKRAS MAGEA6-expressing cells in Dulbecco Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) without fetal bovine serum (FBS), glucose, or glutamine (DMEM–) for 5 hr robustly downregulated MAGEA6 expression (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: DMEM supplemented with carbon sources of glucose or glutamine partially rescued MAGEA6 protein levels.
source: In contrast, DMEM– supplemented with carbon sources of glucose or glutamine partially rescued MAGEA6, while DMEM– containing FBS or both carbon sources fully recovered MAGEA6 levels in both short (5 hr) (Figure 4E) and long (24 hr) (Figure 4F) term culture conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4E and 4F.

claim: DMEM containing FBS or both carbon sources fully recovered MAGEA6 levels in both short and long term culture conditions.
source: In contrast, DMEM– supplemented with carbon sources of glucose or glutamine partially rescued MAGEA6, while DMEM– containing FBS or both carbon sources fully recovered MAGEA6 levels in both short (5 hr) (Figure 4E) and long (24 hr) (Figure 4F) term culture conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4E and 4F.

claim: MAGEA6 expression is nutrient sensitive.
source: The rapid, highly synchronized changes in MAGEA6 expression and S6K phosphorylation status confirmed that MAGEA6 expression is nutrient sensitive.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the coordinated changes in MAGEA6 and S6K phosphorylation under nutrient depletion.

claim: MAGEA6 protein levels are not regulated by the AKT/mTORC1 pathway.
source: To examine whether MAGEA6 protein stability is maintained by mTORC1, we treated HPDE-iKRAS MAGEA6-expressing cells with rapamycin and MK2206 to inhibit mTORC1 or its upstream kinase AKT1, respectively. We did not observe any change in MAGEA6 protein amount after either treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), suggesting that MAGEA6 protein levels are not regulated by the AKT/mTORC1 pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis with AKT and mTORC1 inhibitors shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Addition of MG132 to starved HPDE-iKRAS cells fully rescued MAGEA6 from degradation.
source: Consistent with a role of ubiquitination for protein degradation regulation, addition of MG132 to the starved HPDE-iKRAS cells (Figure 4G) and other PDAC lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) fully rescued MAGEA6 from degradation.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Cancer-specific mutations and carbon source depletion induce MAGEA6 degradation by proteasomes.
source: In summary, our data show that cancer-specific mutations and carbon source depletion induce MAGEA6 degradation by proteasomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments showing MG132 rescue of MAGEA6 under mutation and nutrient depletion conditions.

claim: HPDE-iKRAS, AsPC-1, and MIA PaCa-2 cells stably expressing wild-type MAGEA6 showed reduced AMPK phosphorylation on Thr172 and increased S6K phosphorylation on Thr389.
source: In agreement with the reported autophagy inhibitory role of MAGEA3/6 (Pineda et al., 2015), HPDE-iKRAS, AsPC-1, and MIA PaCa-2 cells stably expressing wild-type MAGEA6 showed reduced AMPK phosphorylation on Thr172 and increased S6K phosphorylation on Thr389 (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining of LC3B in MAGEA6-expressing HPDE cells treated with bafilomycin A1 dramatically reduced the cell population with a high number of LC3B puncta.
source: Immunofluorescence staining of LC3B in MAGEA6–expressing HPDE cells treated with lysosome inhibitor bafilomycin A1 (BafA1) dramatically reduced the cell population with a high number of LC3B puncta (Figure 5B), suggesting slower autophagosome formation and thus lower basal autophagy activity levels in these cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 5B with p=0.002.

claim: MAGEA6 expression suggests slower autophagosome formation and lower basal autophagy activity levels.
source: Immunofluorescence staining of LC3B in MAGEA6–expressing HPDE cells treated with lysosome inhibitor bafilomycin A1 (BafA1) dramatically reduced the cell population with a high number of LC3B puncta (Figure 5B), suggesting slower autophagosome formation and thus lower basal autophagy activity levels in these cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the reduced LC3B puncta in MAGEA6-expressing cells.

claim: Autophagic flux study using BafA1 showed slower SQSTM1/p62 accumulation in MAGEA6-expressing cells compared with control cells.
source: Autophagic flux study using BafA1 showed slower SQSTM1/p62 accumulation in MAGEA6-expressing cells compared with control cells (Figure 5C, left), suggesting a slower turnover of SQSTM1/p62 and therefore further supporting the anti-autophagy role of MAGEA6.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Cells expressing MAGEA6H305fs* and MAGEA6N254I showed minimal changes in autophagy signaling compared with control cells.
source: Importantly, cells expressing MAGEA6H305fs* and MAGEA6N254I, which are susceptible to proteasome mediated degradation, showed minimal changes in autophagy signaling (Figure 5A), autophagosome formation (Figure 5B), and autophagic flux (Figure 5C, right and Figure 5—figure supplement 2) compared with control cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple autophagy assays shown in Figure 5A, 5B, 5C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Short-term culture of HPDE-iKRAS cells in DMEM– showed a gradual reduction in MAGEA6 expression, although MAGEA6 levels still remained sufficient to suppress AMPK Thr172 phosphorylation.
source: In nutrient-deficient conditions, short-term culture of HPDE-iKRAS cells in DMEM– showed a gradual reduction in MAGEA6 expression, although MAGEA6 levels still remained sufficient to suppress AMPK Thr172 phosphorylation, reduce induction of LC3B expression (Figure 5D) and to impair autophagic flux, as demonstrated by the slow accumulation of SQSTM1/p62 and LC3B in the presence of BafA1 (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: Long-term culture (24 hr) of cells expressing wild-type MAGEA6 in DMEM– completely abolished MAGEA6 expression and thus allowed autophagy re-initiation.
source: Nevertheless, long-term culture (24 hr) of cells expressing wild-type MAGEA6 in DMEM– completely abolished MAGEA6 expression and thus allowed autophagy re-initiation, as indicated by low S6K Thr389 and high AMPK Thr172 phosphorylation (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: MAGEA6 suppresses both basal and short-term starvation-induced autophagy in PDAC.
source: In summary, MAGEA6 suppresses both basal and short-term starvation-induced autophagy in PDAC.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple autophagy assays under basal and nutrient-deficient conditions.

claim: MAGEA6's autophagy-quenching effect is revoked when MAGEA6 is downregulated either by degradation-prone mutation or by long-term starvation-induced protein degradation.
source: Its autophagy-quenching effect is revoked when MAGEA6 is downregulated either by degradation-prone mutation or by long-term starvation-induced protein degradation.
evidence: The claim is supported by autophagy assays showing restoration of autophagy when MAGEA6 is degraded.

claim: MAGEA6 expression transformed HPDE cells and induced xenograft tumor growth.
source: In consonance with its role in autophagy suppression, MAGEA6 expression transformed HPDE cells, induced xenograft tumor growth (Figure 6A), and led to poor survival (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by xenograft assay results shown in Figure 6A with p=0.016.

claim: MAGEA6 expression led to poor survival in xenograft mouse models.
source: In consonance with its role in autophagy suppression, MAGEA6 expression transformed HPDE cells, induced xenograft tumor growth (Figure 6A), and led to poor survival (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 6B with p=0.0494.

claim: There was no association between endogenous MAGEA6 and p53 expression in HPDE-iKRAS or in six other PDAC cell lines.
source: However, we did not find any association between endogenous MAGEA6 and p53 expression in HPDE-iKRAS or in six other PDAC cell lines (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR and immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ectopic expression of MAGEA6 variants in BxPC-3 and MIA PaCa-2 lines did not induce changes in p53 protein levels.
source: Furthermore, ectopic expression of MAGEA6 variants in the BxPC-3 and MIA PaCa-2 lines did not induce changes in p53 protein levels in the presence or absence of the proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that MAGEA6 drives PDAC independently of p53.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: MAGEA6 drives PDAC independently of p53.
source: Furthermore, ectopic expression of MAGEA6 variants in the BxPC-3 and MIA PaCa-2 lines did not induce changes in p53 protein levels in the presence or absence of the proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that MAGEA6 drives PDAC independently of p53.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of p53 changes upon MAGEA6 expression.

claim: Knockdown of MAGEA6 in BxPC-3 dramatically increased tumor volume compared with xenografts without MAGEA6 knockdown.
source: In agreement with the anti-tumorigenic role of MAGEA6 at a late disease stage, knockdown of MAGEA6 in the transformed PDAC cell line BxPC-3, which has high endogenous wild-type MAGEA6 expression, dramatically increased tumor volume compared with xenografts without MAGEA6 knockdown (Figure 6C top and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by xenograft assay results shown in Figure 6C with p values of 0.016 and 0.001.

claim: Immunohistochemical staining of BxPC-3 tumors revealed a robust decrease in LC3B levels in the MAGEA6 knockdown cohort.
source: Immunohistochemical staining of the BxPC-3 tumors revealed a robust decrease in LC3B levels and, thus, elevated autophagy activity in the MAGEA6 knockdown cohort (Figure 6C bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 6C bottom.

claim: Knockdown of ATG7 and VPS34 suppressed tumor growth induced by MAGEA6 downregulation.
source: In support of this contention, knockdown of ATG7 and VPS34, key players for autophagy activation, suppressed tumor growth induced by MAGEA6 downregulation, consistent with autophagy activity playing a key role in promoting tumor growth in response to MAGEA6 depletion in BxPC-3 (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by xenograft assay results shown in Figure 6D with p values of 0.51 and 0.90.

claim: Autophagy activity plays a key role in promoting tumor growth in response to MAGEA6 depletion in BxPC-3.
source: In support of this contention, knockdown of ATG7 and VPS34, key players for autophagy activation, suppressed tumor growth induced by MAGEA6 downregulation, consistent with autophagy activity playing a key role in promoting tumor growth in response to MAGEA6 depletion in BxPC-3 (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the suppression of tumor growth by autophagy gene knockdown.

claim: Approximately one-third of MAGEA6 mutation events (6/17) found in the ICGC lung cancer database displayed reduced protein expression.
source: We reasoned that lung cancer is a better option for evaluating the impact of MAGEA6 on different stages of cancer development (initiation and progression) because (1) a large number of patients with lung cancer showed high MAGEA6 expression and mutation events, and (2) approximately one-third of MAGEA6 mutation events (6/17) found in the ICGC lung cancer database displayed reduced protein expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot and qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: A Kaplan-Meier survival analysis of 889 patients with lung cancer showed a significant association of high MAGEA6 expression and poor overall survival in cancers at stage I (hazard ratio = 1.96, p<0.0001).
source: A Kaplan-Meier survival analysis of 889 patients with lung cancer showed a significant association of high MAGEA6 expression and poor overall survival in cancers at stage I (hazard ratio = 1.96, p<0.0001) but not in those at stage II (hazard ratio = 1.1, p=0.6088) or stage III (hazard ratio = 1.06, p=0.8441) (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 6E using data from Győrffy et al., 2013.

claim: High MAGEA6 expression was not significantly associated with poor overall survival in stage II lung cancer (hazard ratio = 1.1, p=0.6088).
source: A Kaplan-Meier survival analysis of 889 patients with lung cancer showed a significant association of high MAGEA6 expression and poor overall survival in cancers at stage I (hazard ratio = 1.96, p<0.0001) but not in those at stage II (hazard ratio = 1.1, p=0.6088) or stage III (hazard ratio = 1.06, p=0.8441) (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: High MAGEA6 expression was not significantly associated with poor overall survival in stage III lung cancer (hazard ratio = 1.06, p=0.8441).
source: A Kaplan-Meier survival analysis of 889 patients with lung cancer showed a significant association of high MAGEA6 expression and poor overall survival in cancers at stage I (hazard ratio = 1.96, p<0.0001) but not in those at stage II (hazard ratio = 1.1, p=0.6088) or stage III (hazard ratio = 1.06, p=0.8441) (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Wild-type and mutant MAGEA6 play distinct roles to promote tumor initiation and development at different disease stages.
source: Collectively, our in vivo data and the patient survival analysis strongly support the hypothesis that wild-type and mutant MAGEA6 play distinct roles to promote tumor initiation and development at different disease stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by xenograft experiments and patient survival analysis.

claim: Intact MAGEA6 suppresses autophagy, which can be oncogenic in early-stage disease when low autophagy activity is preferred.
source: Our study showed that a high number of MAGEA variants identified in pan-cancer analyses were associated with reduced protein expression, suggesting that the impact of these MAGEA gene mutations on potential and MAGEA directed cancer immunotherapy may need further evaluation. In our investigation of the relationship between MAGEA6 and autophagy, we found that intact MAGEA6 suppresses autophagy, which can be oncogenic in early-stage disease when low autophagy activity is preferred (Kimmelman, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by autophagy assays and is cited to Kimmelman, 2011.

claim: The degradation of MAGEA6 through ubiquitin proteasome pathway in late-stage disease revokes autophagy and further promotes cancer progression.
source: The degradation of MAGEA6 through ubiquitin proteasome pathway in late-stage disease revokes autophagy and further promotes cancer progression (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by xenograft experiments and autophagy assays, and is illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Impairment of proteasome activity led to activation of the autophagy pathway.
source: For example, previous studies identified multiple protein substrates targeted by the autophagy and ubiquitin proteasome pathways (Milani et al., 2009; Pandey et al., 2007). Further analysis showed that impairment of proteasome activity led to activation of the autophagy pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Milani et al., 2009 and Pandey et al., 2007.

claim: The crosstalk between autophagy and ubiquitin proteasome pathways is believed to be a potential compensatory mechanism allowing cells to reduce levels of ubiquitinated substrates and provide tumorigenic advantages.
source: The crosstalk between these two systems is believed to be a potential compensatory mechanism allowing cells to reduce levels of ubiquitinated substrates and provide tumorigenic advantages.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about cellular catabolism.

claim: MAGEA2, A3, A6, and C2 bind to the TRIM28 E3 ligase with similar strength and boost ubiquitin ligase activity against p53.
source: For example, MAGEA2, A3, A6, and C2 were shown to bind to the TRIM28 E3 ligase with similar strength and to boost ubiquitin ligase activity against p53 (Doyle et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Doyle et al., 2010.

claim: MAGEA3 and MAGEA6 are believed to work complementarily to regulate TRIM28 E3 activity and autophagy suppression.
source: Indeed, MAGEA3 and MAGEA6 are believed to work complementarily to regulate TRIM28 E3 activity and autophagy suppression (Pineda et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pineda et al., 2015.

claim: Inhibition of autophagy using 3-methyladenine sensitizes cells to cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil in esophageal and colon cancers, respectively.
source: Inhibition of autophagy using 3-methyladenine sensitizes cells to cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil in esophageal and colon cancers, respectively (Li et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2009 and Liu et al., 2011.

claim: Co-treatment of gemcitabine with 3-methyladenine, the AMPK inhibitor compound C, or the lysosomal inhibitor chloroquine potentiates gemcitabine-induced apoptosis in PDAC cells.
source: In PDAC cells, co-treatment of gemcitabine (the first-line therapy in the clinic) with 3-methyladenine, the AMPK inhibitor compound C, or the lysosomal inhibitor chloroquine potentiates gemcitabine-induced apoptosis (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2016.

claim: Recent PDAC studies demonstrated autophagy activation when KRAS or the downstream ERK pathway is suppressed.
source: Recent PDAC studies also demonstrated autophagy activation when KRAS or the downstream ERK pathway is suppressed and pharmacologic inhibition of autophagy regulators synergistically enhanced the ERK inhibitors-induced antitumor activity in KRAS-driven PDAC (Bryant et al., 2019; Kinsey et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bryant et al., 2019 and Kinsey et al., 2019.

claim: Pharmacologic inhibition of autophagy regulators synergistically enhanced the ERK inhibitors-induced antitumor activity in KRAS-driven PDAC.
source: Recent PDAC studies also demonstrated autophagy activation when KRAS or the downstream ERK pathway is suppressed and pharmacologic inhibition of autophagy regulators synergistically enhanced the ERK inhibitors-induced antitumor activity in KRAS-driven PDAC (Bryant et al., 2019; Kinsey et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bryant et al., 2019 and Kinsey et al., 2019.

claim: PDAC tumors expressing high level of MAGEA6 may be more sensitive to cytotoxic agents due to the low autophagy activity.
source: For example, PDAC tumors expressing high level of MAGEA6 may be more sensitive to cytotoxic agents due to the low autophagy activity while tumors harboring MAGEA6 degradation-prone mutations may show increased dependency on autophagy, and thus by more susceptible to treatment with an autophagy inhibitor.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on the findings about MAGEA6's role in autophagy suppression.

claim: Tumors harboring MAGEA6 degradation-prone mutations may show increased dependency on autophagy, and thus be more susceptible to treatment with an autophagy inhibitor.
source: For example, PDAC tumors expressing high level of MAGEA6 may be more sensitive to cytotoxic agents due to the low autophagy activity while tumors harboring MAGEA6 degradation-prone mutations may show increased dependency on autophagy, and thus by more susceptible to treatment with an autophagy inhibitor.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on the findings about MAGEA6 degradation and autophagy reactivation.

claim: Cancer/testis antigens (CTAs) are encoded by genes whose expression is normally restricted to male germ cells but is de-repressed in various human cancers.
source: Cancer/testis antigens (CTAs) are encoded by genes whose expression is normally restricted to male germ cells but is de-repressed in various human cancers (Chen et al., 2017; Hofmann et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2017 and Hofmann et al., 2008.

claim: The aberrant expression of Type 1 MAGEs in cancer is a result of promoter hypomethylation due to genome-wide epigenetic reprogramming.
source: The aberrant expression of Type 1 MAGEs in cancer is a result of promoter hypomethylation due to genome-wide epigenetic reprogramming.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about MAGE gene regulation.

claim: High MAGEA protein expression has been associated with advanced stage in multiple cancer lineages.
source: Consistent with a role in tumor progression, high MAGEA protein expression has been associated with advanced stage (Liu et al., 2008; Sang et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2016) and poor prognosis (Weon and Potts, 2015; Xu et al., 2014; Zhai et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2015) in multiple cancer lineages.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2008; Sang et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2016.

claim: High MAGEA protein expression has been associated with poor prognosis in multiple cancer lineages.
